name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming voters dodged a big-time bullet by defeating Prop 1
description:
If the state had approved a 50% residential property tax cut, it would suffer a major loss of essential services, columnist Kerry Drake opines.
The post Wyoming voters dodged a big-time bullet by defeating Prop 1 appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming didn’t catch any part of that mighty blue wave that washed over much of the country in Tuesday’s midterm election, but I don’t think anyone seriously thought it would.

Opinion

It did, however, dodge a major bullet by rejecting a dud of an idea that would have resulted in major cuts to essential services throughout the state. Wyoming communities could not have absorbed that much pain.
The Equality State did what it’s done in most elections for years: send an all-Republican congressional delegation back to Washington, D.C., elect a slate of GOP state officeholders and put Republican supermajorities in both houses of the Legislature.
But in one vital nonpartisan area, Wyoming voters came together and scored a smashing victory over an attempt to cut most residential property taxes by a whopping 50%.
If the Proposition 1 initiative had passed Tuesday, opponents said Wyoming could have lost $125 million a year or more in property tax revenue, resulting in major cuts to essential services, including law enforcement, fire protection, emergency medical services, hospitals, schools, roads and bridges.
And that revenue would have just disappeared; the initiative didn’t provide any means to replace it. During previous legislative discussions about either cutting property taxes by 50% or eliminating them altogether, some lawmakers had proposed increasing the state sales tax to “backfill” the lost revenue.
Fortunately, Prop 1 failed. According to unofficial final results, 58% of voters opposed or didn’t vote on Prop 1, while a total of 42% backed the measure. If a voter left the question blank, it was counted as a “no” vote.
This misguided idea was the brainchild of three people: Brent Bien, who was endorsed by the Wyoming Republican Party but finished third in this year’s GOP gubernatorial primary; his former campaign manager, Rich Weber, and ex-Wyoming Republican Party state committeewoman Cheryl Aguiar.



Two years ago this trio began a movement to get the massive tax exemption on the ballot for the 2024 election. While they failed to collect enough signatures to make the deadline, Secretary of State Chuck Gray certified the initiative for 2026 after his office verified more than 30,000 signatures of registered voters in January 2025.
It was a stunning accomplishment, the first citizen’s initiative to be placed on a Wyoming ballot in 30 years. One of the reasons for the extreme dry spell is because the state has such a high bar for ballot initiatives, which must obtain signatures equal to 15% of the votes cast in the previous general election’s U.S. House race.
Moreover, the signatures must come from registered voters in at least two-thirds of the state’s 23 counties, which is 16 counties.
The Legislature has rejected attempts to lower the bar, obviously because lawmakers want to make the laws, and not turn that power directly over to voters. 
In the case of the long-winded “People’s Initiative to Limit Property Tax in Wyoming Through a Homeowner’s Property Exemption,” it initially appeared to many political observers as one issue that had a great chance of passing.
Within a few months after its ballot certification, I heard of — but did not specifically see — polling data that found more than 80% of the state’s likely voters viewed the initiative favorably. I didn’t doubt it.
For people who understood what a dangerous impact such action could have on property tax revenue that goes directly to local governments, special districts and public schools, it appeared potentially devastating.
One of the reasons is because lawmakers in the far-right Freedom Caucus had seemingly convinced the public that passing tax cuts was imperative due to major tax increases that had swept through much of the state.
As home values rose, residential property taxes during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2022 increased by an average of 16%, compared to prior years when annual hikes were 3% to 4%. During the same time of double-digit property tax increases throughout the state, Teton County — the wealthiest county in the nation — saw a 36% increase due to skyrocketing house values.
Some Freedom Caucus members in the House and their Senate allies claimed some homeowners would lose their property unless the Legislature provided some so-called “tax relief.” They made this claim without producing any real-life examples of anyone that would happen to, but the narrative was quickly ingrained by politicians and their constituents as gospel.
In the 2024 election, the Freedom Caucus saw enough members elected to take control of the House. The leadership immediately went to work on bills to cut residential property taxes.
One new law capped the annual increase at 4%. A tax rebate program was expanded. For homeowners of more than 25 years, a temporary 25% tax cut was passed, then made permanent.
These measures had started to work. At the same time, the rapid increases in home values began to subside. Meanwhile, the Freedom Caucus had clearly lost the support of voters in the Aug. 18 Republican primary, as it was booted out of House control and its much-ballyhooed attempt to take over the Senate fizzled.
The cries for property tax cuts died too. Two months before Tuesday’s general election, the Joint Revenue Committee said no to a proposed bill to eliminate residential property taxes that it had approved the previous year. In 2025, the bill died when the House ran out of time to consider it.
The panel’s decision came amid the release of new data showing that the majority of Wyoming homeowners did not take advantage of the 25% property tax cut that the Legislature had approved without any income restrictions.
Clearly, the ballot initiative would have only paved the way for the rich to get richer, while people who owned modest homes would receive a small tax cut.
People had stopped coming to legislative committee meetings demanding that property taxes be cut. During the Joint Revenue Committee’s meeting on sponsoring a bill to let voters amend the Wyoming Constitution by eliminating residential property taxes and a companion measure to backfill it with higher sales taxes, no one spoke for or against the measure.
That particularly pleased Rep. Liz Storer, D-Jackson, who asked the panel, “What is the purpose of these bills, and why would we take the time to continue to move them forward, also given that I do not think they will be met with success in the next Legislature? So help me understand your reasoning.”
No one could.

Between August and the beginning of October, school districts in the state spent[...]
text:
North Carolina school buses are ready to roll out for the start of the 2025-26 school year. (Photo: NCDPI) Transportation spending for school districts has nearly doubled this school year as diesel prices have reached record highs. Now, the North Carolina Department of Public Instruction is asking lawmakers for a one-time $40 million fund to help districts cover the additional costs.
Between August and the beginning of October, school districts in the state spent $17.1 million on 3.8 million gallons of diesel fuel. That’s nearly double the $8.6 million they spent for 3.6 million gallons during the same period last school year, according to data DPI presented to the State Board of Education on Wednesday. Districts also spent $8.6 million on 3.7 million gallons during the same period in the 2024-25 school year.
“We were seeing that school districts are spending about twice as much on fuel in the first couple of months of the school year as they were in the previous two school years, even though they bought the same amount of gallons,” Geoff Coltrane, DPI’s senior director of government affairs and strategy, told board members. 
The money would help districts cover fuel costs above the roughly $3 per gallon included in their transportation funding allocation. It would be distributed to school districts and charter schools based on need, Coltrane said.
Diesel prices in North Carolina hit a record average of more than $6 per gallon earlier this fall, putting so much pressure on school transportation budgets that some district leaders said they may be forced to make cuts elsewhere or use money from their reserves.
NC Gov Stein signs gas tax holiday into law

Last month, the General Assembly suspended the state’s motor fuel tax, including the tax on diesel, through Nov. 30. But the suspension doesn’t help school districts because they’re already exempt from fuel taxes.
The department has already begun sharing the request with lawmakers and legislative staff, Coltrane said. DPI did not provide an estimate of how much individual districts could receive.
Democrats won control of the state House in Tuesday’s midterm elections for the first time since 2010, while Republicans retained a narrow majority in the Senate.
The proposal was part of a broader package of budget priorities DPI presented to the State Board of Education. The department plans to submit its recommendations to the state budget office by early January for consideration in the governor’s budget.
Among the other requests, DPI is seeking $300 million in each year of the two-year budget to help school districts buy new literacy and math instructional materials aligned with recently adopted standards. The department is also asking for $115 million to help districts replace student devices, after a report found that many districts don’t have enough money to replace them.
DPI is also seeking $117 million to increase funding for needs-based school construction grants, and another $25 million for school repairs and renovations. The department wants to increase funding for school health personnel by 20%, which it estimates could help districts hire about 700 additional counselors, nurses, social workers and psychologists.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: School meals focus shifts to North Dakota Legislature after Measure 2 defeat
description: An attempt to guarantee free school meals to K-12 students narrowly failed at the ballot box Tuesday, but the issue isn’t going away in North Dakota.  Supporters and opponents of Measure 2, the defeated constitutional amendment, are looking ahead to next steps. Nearly 51% of voters rejected the measure, while about 49% supported it, according […]
text:
Students eat lunch at Roosevelt Elementary School in Bismarck on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)An attempt to guarantee free school meals to K-12 students narrowly failed at the ballot box Tuesday, but the issue isn’t going away in North Dakota. 
Supporters and opponents of Measure 2, the defeated constitutional amendment, are looking ahead to next steps. Nearly 51% of voters rejected the measure, while about 49% supported it, according to complete but unofficial results.
Sen. Paul Thomas, R-Velva, said Wednesday he thinks there is unanimous support in the state for the core principle of ensuring no child goes hungry. 
“Nobody in North Dakota feels or has any belief that a child should ever not be fed,” said Thomas, who opposed the initiated measure but supports legislative action. “This really isn’t a partisan Republican-Democrat divided issue.”
Voters defeat free school meal ballot measure in North Dakota

An advocate for free school meals in the Legislature said she plans to introduce legislation in 2027 to accomplish what Measure 2 failed to do. 
Rep. LaurieBeth Hager, D-Fargo, the sponsor of a free school meals bill that failed to advance in 2025, said she plans to introduce similar legislation again to require all K-12 schools to offer breakfast and lunch to students at no cost. 
“It’s equalizing the kids. We don’t charge them differently for books. We don’t charge them differently for using the buses,” Hager said. “It’s part of the school day and part of the learning experience.”
Hager said she believes the fact that Measure 2 was a constitutional amendment likely scared off voters who are otherwise supportive of providing free school meals to K-12 students.
“If the powers that be think this needs to be in statute instead of in the constitution, then we will get it done that way,” Hager said. “The fight continues.”
Opponents of the measure, including Gov. Kelly Armstrong, criticized putting school meals in the constitution. The program was estimated to cost $124.3 million to $134.3 million every two years starting in 2027-29. Critics said mandating that spending in the constitution would tie lawmakers’ hands during lean budget years.
Armstrong said Wednesday he doesn’t anticipate a large push by Republican lawmakers to revisit a universal school meals program.
“I just think it’s a little harder politically today than it would have been even six months ago,” he said.
Rep. Mike Nathe, R-Bismarck, said voters rejected Measure 2, and he questioned why state lawmakers would consider going against the voters’ wishes.
“The people of North Dakota spoke. They rejected Measure 2, and we have to respect that,” Nathe said. “But that does not mean we can’t work around the edges a little bit and kind of make some things better.”
Nathe sponsored a school meal bill in the January special session that aimed to head off a constitutional ballot measure. House lawmakers approved the bill, but it lost in the Senate by two votes.
Thomas said he does not support a statutory free school meals bill like Hager’s proposal, but the senator said the election result shows voters expect lawmakers will continue working on the issue.
“They want us to continue working on some of the shortcomings of current policy,” Thomas said.
Thomas is working on policy ideas he plans to introduce in the legislative session that begins in January. His bill is being drafted and he plans to gauge his colleagues’ interest when the Legislative Management committee meets next week. 
Other lawmakers, including Rep. Chuck Walen, R-New Town, have said they plan to propose alternative solutions on school meals. Sen. Michelle Axtman, R-Bismarck, said the issue has not been “put to bed,” and expects to make progress during the session.
“I think we’ll find a way to maximize federal dollars and be very strategic and problem-solving to come up with a solution that makes more sense than the measure did,” Axtman said in an interview Tuesday night.
North Dakota families can face debt collections if they can’t afford school lunch

While North Dakota lawmakers have voted against free school meal bills, they have adopted other proposals including an anti-lunch shaming bill in 2023. However, more than two dozen school districts reported in a survey that they refer families to collection agencies for unpaid lunch debt.
Legislators also have slightly expanded how many students qualify for free and reduced lunch through the federal program. In 2025, lawmakers earmarked $6 million to raise the income level used to determine families’ eligibility. 
About $2.5 million of that funding was spent in the first half of the 2025-27 budget cycle, said Lynelle Johnson, director of the Office of Child Nutrition and Food Distribution for the North Dakota Department of Public Instruction. The funding has helped about 3,000 students who would not have otherwise qualified under the federal free and reduced lunch income eligibility requirements. 
“That additional expanded eligibility is very appreciated,” Johnson said.
Robin Nelson, chair of Together for School Meals, said many North Dakotans gave their “time, energy and heart” to the Measure 2 campaign because they saw a need in their schools and communities. 
“We wish we could have given North Dakota families better news. They are why we took on this effort, and they remain our concern as we consider what comes next,” Nelson said. 
Amy Jacobson, the group’s spokesperson, said members of the coalition are going to take time to digest the results and consult with stakeholders before they make any decisions on what they will focus on moving forward. 
“Families are still stretching their budgets, and children still need meals to get through the school day ready to learn,” Jacobson said.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com. Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

title: Virginia voters split on 1% sales tax for school construction
description: On Election Day, out of 47 Virginia localities, about 30% authorized their governments to collect a 1% sales tax to address rising school construction costs, while about 70% did not.  In June, state lawmakers authorized localities, pending voter support, to raise revenue for school construction and modernization with a 1% sales tax. The state estimates […]
text:
An early view of the school construction work in Halifax County. (Photo courtesy of Halifax County Public Schools)On Election Day, out of 47 Virginia localities, about 30% authorized their governments to collect a 1% sales tax to address rising school construction costs, while about 70% did not. 
In June, state lawmakers authorized localities, pending voter support, to raise revenue for school construction and modernization with a 1% sales tax. The state estimates over 1000 school buildings are more than 50 years old, and would take $25 billion to rebuild or improve. 
House Education Committee Chair Sam Rasoul, D-Roanoke, and Sen. Jeremy McPike, D-Prince William, proposed the idea last January. Both measures were ultimately added to the state’s budget.
“School construction is a critical need,” said McPike ahead of the results. “This is a direct question to the voters in the form of a referendum, and it’s up to the voters to decide how they want to fund school construction.”
Tuesday’s results are expected to help 14 localities move the needle on school modernization, while leaving questions about the 33 that rejected the opportunity and what comes next.

Rasoul said the idea was to help address billions in school construction needs in the commonwealth. But citizens have raised concerns about tax increases, a point former Gov. Glenn Youngkin raised in previous years
Mecklenburg, one of the nine localities with state-approved authority, has not put the matter to voters since receiving authorization, largely because it opposed raising taxes, according to Board of Supervisors’ records in 2021. 
Mecklenburg estimated it would need about $6 million per year in debt payments to move forward with new school construction, which ultimately dampened interest in adding the option to ballots. 
In addition, the county had already invested in newer additions to the three elementary schools. 
No action has been taken since former state Sen. Frank Ruff successfully proposed the change in 2020.
In 2019, Halifax County became the first locality to receive authority from the state, which is required since Virginia is a “Dillon’s Rule” state, meaning local governments can only exercise powers granted by the state legislature. 
Localities can adjust property tax rates, but they need General Assembly approval to change sales taxes.
With the election’s results, the list has grown from the original nine — city of Danville and the counties of Charlotte, Gloucester, Halifax, Henry, Mecklenburg, Northampton, Patrick and Pittsylvania — to 23 locations.
Rasoul acknowledged that, while he championed the bill, it is not a long-term solution to the state’s school construction needs. Additional support, particularly at the state level, will be necessary to help struggling school divisions, he said.
“This isn’t going to be able to build all the schools that need to be built,” Rasoul said. “So there’s a lot more that needs to be done … even at the state level to help struggling school divisions.”
McPike said upcoming discussions with his colleagues on the Commission on School Construction and Modernization should focus on analyzing the referendum results once they are available, evaluating long-term funding structures for school construction and reviewing stabilized projections over time.
The commission and all state lawmakers will return to Richmond on Jan. 13, 2027 to discuss future legislation and budget amendments.

title: Barre voters approve school district budget on fourth attempt
description:
The $56.6 million budget approved Tuesday notably makes cuts to open staff positions and facilities expenses while maintaining funds for sports. The district is the last in the state to approve an annual spending plan. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Barre voters approve school district budget on fourth attempt.
text:
The Barre City Elementary and Middle School seen on Tuesday, August 8, 2023.  File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

BARRE — Voters in the Barre Unified Union School District approved an annual spending plan for the district on their fourth attempt Tuesday. 
The district was the last in the state to approve a budget, which allocates $56.6 million this school year. Residents across Barre Town and Barre City previously voted down three costlier proposed spending plans. 
Notably, the district’s new budget approves cuts to office staff, open positions and facilities expenses. It spares cuts to winter sports and after school activities, which board members previously said might be on the chopping block after the last budget failed in September. 
Across both municipalities, 58% of voters approved the latest spending plan, according to totals from Barre Town’s website and Barre City’s clerk.
The drawn-out process of approving the district’s budget is notable because the district has among the lowest rates of per-student spending in the state. Still, voters rejected a $57.8 million budget on Town Meeting Day and have rejected two smaller proposed budgets since then. 
When students went back to school without a voter-approved budget for the district, board members said the district had to take out a line of credit, a measure expected to cost the district up to $22,000 in monthly interest payments. 
This story will be updated.

name: WyoFile
title: No new property tax cut: Wyoming voters defeat Proposition 1
description:
Result comes after opponents warned citizens initiative would decimate local budgets for counties, special districts and education. 
The post No new property tax cut: Wyoming voters defeat Proposition 1 appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming voters on Tuesday defeated Proposition 1, a sweeping tax relief ballot initiative that opponents warned would devastate budgets for local county governments, special districts and education. 
Though it came to the ballot with more than 30,000 signatures, the measure’s defeat illustrates the appetite for drastic property tax cuts did not extend to a majority of voters on Election Day. 
Proposition 1 would have exempted 50% of a primary residence’s assessed value from property taxation, resulting in annual property tax revenue decreases estimated at anywhere from $92.6 million to $124.8 million. 
The measure needed approval from more than 50% of those voting in the general election to pass. Ballots left blank counted as no votes.
As of 11:15 p.m. Tuesday, AP results showed that with two-thirds of the vote counted, 55% of voters opposing Prop 1, with 42% backing the measure. Laramie and Sweetwater counties were not included in that total, but results in those counties showed Prop 1 failing by similar or larger margins.
A yard sign photographed Oct. 29, 2026 in Lander urges people to vote against Proposition 1. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
Its loss comes on the heels of a well-funded and organized movement to defeat Proposition 1. Opponents ranged from organizations such as the Wyoming Hospitals Association and the Wyoming Education Association to prominent figures like former Gov. Dave Freudenthal, a Democrat, and Republican Gov. Mark Gordon. 
“The voters have spoken and tonight was a big win for the hard-working families of Wyoming,” Kim Amen, chair of the Vote No on Prop 1 Coalition, said in a statement. “We hope and trust that state lawmakers will listen to the will of the voters, who said loudly that critical services like our public schools, first responders, road repairs, and libraries should receive the funding they need and that Wyoming families deserve.”
The Wyoming Taxpayers Association — which bills itself as Wyoming’s “tax watchdog” — was among critics. That’s because Proposition 1 would have weakened Wyoming’s economy, disproportionately hurt counties not rich in minerals and forced reductions in essential services, the association said in campaign materials.
If Proposition 1 had passed, counties like Lincoln, Park and Fremont would have faced revenue cuts of more than 40%, according to the association.  
“Prop 1 is not sound fiscal policy,” reads a post from the association’s website. 
Homeowner relief vs. local budgets
Proposition 1 was among a raft of efforts to relieve property owners after COVID-era real estate trends pushed up residential values. That resulted in spiking tax bills for many Wyoming homeowners; increases varied by county. In Park County, the average homeowner saw their tax bills jump over 60% in three years. 
In October of 2023, two-time gubernatorial candidate Brent Bien, along with his former campaign manager Rich Weber and former Wyoming Republican Party state committeewoman Cheryl Aguiar, secured approval to begin collecting signatures to get a 50% exemption on the ballot, with no cap on the value.
Secretary of State Chuck Gray certified the initiative in January 2025 after verifying more than 30,000 signatures. 
The numbers indicated high interest — at least when the signature collecting was happening between late 2023 and early 2025. Wyoming lawmakers also passed several property tax relief measures after signature collecting began, including five bills in 2024 and a 2025 bill that created a 25% exemption on the first $1 million of a primary residence’s fair market value.

Some condominiums at Teton Village, the base of Jackson Hole Mountain Resort, are valued at more than $7 million and subject to annual property taxes of almost $50,000. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)

That 25% exemption shrank revenue pools for public education, municipalities and special districts such as hospitals. Some county governments implemented hiring freezes and mandated departmental budget cuts. Some closed libraries, others stopped maintaining parks and many dipped into reserves. 
These results were cast as cautionary tales — examples of painful consequences brought on by property tax cuts. Over the last year, a chorus of opposition has swelled against Proposition 1 — voices that include county treasurers, fire chiefs, education advocates and perhaps most notably, prominent Republicans. 
If Proposition 1 passed, they say, the damages would have spiralled out of control. 
The “Vote No on Prop 1” PAC was well-resourced. Campaign finance filings show nearly $2 million in contributions; the National Education Association has donated $1.4 million. Bien, Weber and Aguiar’s PAC, BCR Voter Initiatives, meanwhile, reported contributions of less than $4,000.
Proposition 1’s supporters, including many who align with the far-right Wyoming Freedom Caucus, said misinformation capitalizing on fear blew the impact of the tax reduction out of proportion. Opponents ignored important nuances of the measure and used a “chicken little” strategy of predicting calamity, Prop 1 supporters argued. 
The loss is another blow to the Freedom Caucus. After years of consolidating power in Wyoming’s Legislature, the bloc in the August primaries lost majority control of the House and backslid in the Senate.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC voters approve all 3 constitutional amendments on ballot
description: North Carolina voters approved all three constitutional amendments on the ballot Tuesday. The amendments authorize lawmakers to impose limits on local governments’ power to raise property taxes, cap the state income tax, and require photo ID for all voters — not just those voting in person. The controversial, Republican-backed property tax amendment was appr[...]
text:
North Carolina voters approved all three constitutional amendments on the ballot Tuesday.
The amendments authorize lawmakers to impose limits on local governments’ power to raise property taxes, cap the state income tax, and require photo ID for all voters — not just those voting in person.
The controversial, Republican-backed property tax amendment was approved with 60% of voters casting votes in favor and 40% against the measure. 
Supporters had predicted voters feeling burdened by local property tax increases would approve the amendment, which GOP lawmakers said is a response to excessively high property taxes. Seniors in particular are cost-burdened by high taxes, they complained.
“Families are getting ripped off as some, but by no means all, local governments rake in billions more than inflation and population growth warrant,” state House Speaker Destin Hall, R-Caldwell, said in the spring.
The amendment gives lawmakers the authority to set a limit on local governments’ ability to increase property taxes by creating a levy limit. But it doesn’t specify how or how much the limit would be. Legislators would work out the details and set the levy limit later, likely in 2027.
Local government officials, progressive advocacy groups and Democratic lawmakers who oppose the measure say state lawmakers already have the authority to do this without a constitutional amendment.
They worry that limiting the amount of tax revenue local governments can collect could have dire consequences for local governments, which could be forced to cut services. Local property taxes help pay for vital needs like public safety, education, and public health.
State income tax amendment
The state income tax amendment was approved with 62% of voters casting votes in favor and 38% against. The amendment establishes a maximum income tax rate of 3.5%. It keeps North Carolina’s income tax rate from being raised higher than 3.5% for personal and corporate income taxes in the future. 
North Carolina’s personal income tax rate stands at 3.99% and it’s slated to fall to 3.49% in 2027.
Supporters of the Republican-backed amendment argued that a higher state income tax makes North Carolina less competitive in attracting business and jobs. 
Sen. Ralph Hise, R-Mitchell, noted that Tennessee, which borders North Carolina, does not have a personal income tax.
Critics argued that the legislature could lower the income tax rate without enshrining the policy in the state constitution.
House Democratic leader Robert Reives of Chatham County said even if the cap on the personal income tax rates passes, costs are still going to be passed on to North Carolinians through fees and sales taxes.
“You’re still getting taxed,” he said in May. “It’s just not coming through personal income tax.”
Photo ID amendment
The photo ID amendment was approved by 60% of voters with 40% voting against.
All voters in the state are already required to show ID when voting in person and by mail, but the photo requirement for mail-in voters was not in the constitution. The amendment enshrines the requirement in the constitution, which makes it more difficult for future legislators to overturn it.
Supporters argued that the Republican-backed amendment creates one standard for all voters, provides an additional identity safeguard and allows lawmakers to enact laws that may include exceptions to the photo ID law.
But critics argued that the amendment is unnecessary because state law already requires a photo ID for mail ballots.
“Really, what this is an effort to make more permanent a commitment to limiting access to the ballot for eligible voters,” Alexander Sirota, executive director of the N.C. Budget and Tax Center, told NC Newsline.

text:
Miranda Jochim of Mandan serves lunch to students at Roosevelt Elementary School in Bismarck on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota voters have rejected a proposed constitutional amendment that sought to guarantee free school meals to all K-12 students in the state. 
Measure 2 was rejected by nearly 51% of voters, according to complete but unofficial results published by the North Dakota Secretary of State’s Office.  
The measure’s margin of defeat was about 2,900 votes. 
Measure 2 was a proposed amendment to the North Dakota constitution that would require schools to provide free lunch and breakfast to K-12 students and be reimbursed by the state for the expense. 
Voters reject higher bar to amend North Dakota’s constitution

The initiated measure was placed on the ballot by a group of sponsoring citizens after the North Dakota Legislature rejected similar proposals in recent legislative sessions. 
The program was estimated to cost $124.3 million to $134.3 million every two years starting in 2027-29, according to the Department of Public Instruction. 
Supporters argued the constitutional requirement will eliminate school meal debts, benefit students’ academic performance and provide financial relief to families across the state.
Opponents including Gov. Kelly Armstrong argued the measure was inappropriate for the state constitution, which is more difficult to change. 
Lawmakers have added state funding to expand how many students qualify for free or reduced lunch, bolstering the federal program. In 2025, lawmakers expanded the free lunch program to include families at 225% of the federal poverty level.
Some lawmakers have raised concerns that the state will lose out on federal dollars if families no longer fill out paperwork for the federal program. A state official has said many students automatically qualify because their families are eligible for other federal programs.
A 2023 law already requires North Dakota schools to provide a meal to students if they request one, even if they don’t have the money to pay, and prohibits any shaming of the student. 
But schools still charge for the meals if the student isn’t signed up for free and reduced lunch programs. Families can face consequences for the debt, such as being referred to debt collection agencies.
School meals are likely to be the subject of debate again during the 2027 legislative session. Some lawmakers have said they prefer a more targeted approach, such as the state paying off school meal debt at the end of a school year. 
Sen. Paul Thomas, R-Velva, has said he plans to propose initiatives ranging from larger portion sizes for school meals and more nutritious options, to trying to help students who go without sufficient meals on the weekends.

title: Louisiana voters approve 7 of 10 constitutional amendments
description: Half of the ballot items involved property taxes that help pay for many parish governments, sheriffs and public schools.
text:
A sign directs voters to the polling location at the East Baton Rouge Public Library Branch in Zachary on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Elise Plunk/Louisiana Illuminator)A ballot with 10 amendments to the Louisiana Constitution was placed before voters statewide on Tuesday’s ballot, and they gave their approval to seven of the proposals.
Half of the ballot items involved property taxes that help pay for many parish governments, sheriffs and public schools.
The voting margins listed were as of 11:15 p.m. Tuesday
Amendment 1: YES – 75%
Amendment 1 gives surviving spouses of deceased disabled veterans to transfer a property tax exemption to a new house. It is expected to affect only a small group of people as just 229 people claimed the existing exemption last year, according to a legislative fiscal analysis.
Amendment 2: NO – 58%
The rejection of Amendment 2 denies local governments the power to remove real estate value assessment deadlines. It would have allowed local governments to keep property tax rates lower for a longer period of time. Under the current system, local officials have said they feel pressure to sometimes raise rates prematurely because if they don’t, they lose the ability to do so in the future. Opponents argued the proposal would create more uncertainty for taxpayers about when their property tax bills would be raised and by how much. 
Amendment 3: YES – 68%
Voters chose to remove the power of judges to grant bail to defendants convicted of certain crimes with minors as victims. The applicable offenses include kidnapping, human trafficking, rape and other sex crimes. Post-conviction bail can be granted at a judge’s discretion before a convicted person reports to prison, such as when their case is on appeal or they are awaiting sentencing. Judges can grant bail except when someone is charged with a crime punishable by death, and there is a high degree of evidence of their guilt. 
Amendment 4: YES – 56%
The provisions of Amendment 4 apply to only two living former Louisiana governors — Democrat John Bel Edwards and Republican Bobby Jindal — and any future holders of the state’s highest office. The amendment prohibits any governor from running for office again once they serve more than one and a half terms, equal to six years. Neither Edwards nor Edwards has expressed interest in running for the office again. 
Amendment 5: NO – 62%
The proposition would have given the Louisiana Legislature the authority to prioritize how the state pays off the debt of its retirement systems when there are surplus funds in the state budget. The existing law that stays in effect requires surplus dollars to go toward the oldest debt first.

Amendment 6: YES – 64%
Local governments can now increase the homestead exemption for many people 65 and older. Voters in the tax jurisdiction must also approve a tax break for seniors through a separate, local ballot initiative. 
Amendment 7: YES – 65%
The statewide vote clears the way for New Orleans to use $152 million in federal funds to replace lead pipes in its drinking water delivery system. Voter approval was needed because there were concerns a state law prohibits the use of that money on private property, though an opinion from Attorney General Liz Murrill had given the go-ahead to do so. The $152 million represents only a small fraction of the $1 billion-plus cost to remove lead pipes from the New Orleans water system. The city is under a 2037 federal deadline to complete the work. 
Amendment 8: YES – 63%
Several states have enacted laws that prohibit a “foreign adversary” or their representative from acquiring or expropriating property. Louisiana is the first to place the prohibition in its state constitution. A state law already prevents these nations from taking over property near military bases as well as buying or leasing any land or immovable property.   
The list of applicable countries currently includes China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia and the former Maduro regime in Venezuela. 
Amendment 9: YES – 59%
Voters approved an increase to the income threshold for people who qualify for a property tax freeze from $100,000 to $150,000. Impacted people are those 65 or older, disabled veterans, other residents who are totally and permanently disabled, and the spouses of military members killed or missing in action. The threshold will be adjusted to match inflation rates in future years. 
Amendment 10: NO – 53%
Voters statewide declined to give their approval for local governments to adopt property tax exemptions for owners who rehabilitate blighted properties. Improvements to derelict homes could have received a tax break of up to 75% of the property’s renovated assessed value for 20 years, and a 25% exemption would have been for remediating vacant land next to a home or business property.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Washington voters embracing income tax on high earners
description: Voters on Tuesday were upholding Washington’s new income tax on households earning more than a million dollars a year, a threshold opponents argued would eventually be lowered to apply to everyone. Initiative 645 to repeal the high-earners tax was failing by an overwhelming margin, 58% to 42%. It lacked support in the state’s most populous […]
text:
Washington state Sen. Jamie Pedersen of Seattle celebrates defeat of an initiative to repeal the income tax on high earners that he wrote and pushed through the Legislature. (Photo by Jacquelyn Jimenez Romero/Washington State Standard)Voters on Tuesday were upholding Washington’s new income tax on households earning more than a million dollars a year, a threshold opponents argued would eventually be lowered to apply to everyone.
Initiative 645 to repeal the high-earners tax was failing by an overwhelming margin, 58% to 42%. It lacked support in the state’s most populous counties on both sides of the state.
In King County, the state’s largest and home to the greatest concentration of Democrats, nearly 67% were voting it down. It was also getting turned down by voters in Skamania, Pacific, Mason and Okanogan counties.
This is a resounding political victory for Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson, whose public embrace of the tax last December was a catalyst for its eventual passage by the Democrat–controlled Legislature.
It also will be a legacy success for Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, an original architect of the tax, who withstood slings and arrows of opponents as he led efforts to massage the content to secure votes up to the final days of session.
“Tonight’s victory is momentous, but there is still more work to do. Defeating I-645 will avoid deep future budget cuts, but in the near term, until the Millionaires Tax is in place, there will still be very difficult decisions ahead in the upcoming legislative session for the governor and legislators,” said Erik Houser, spokesman for the No on 645 campaign.
“But tonight, by saying no to I-645, voters said yes to fiscal responsibility.They said yes to funding core services. They said yes to reforming our upside down tax code to make it more fair for Washington families,” he said.
It is a hard loss for Let’s Go Washington, the conservative political committee founded and funded by hedge fund manager Brian Heywood. His group launched a massive signature-gathering drive to get the initiative on the ballot after the Legislature blocked voters’ ability to erase it with a referendum.
“If the income tax doesn’t get repealed, for the next two years, every job creator that leaves this state, every entrepreneur who doesn’t set up shop in Washington, every employee who is concerned that tax will be lowered to them, that is on Governor Ferguson. This is his income tax,” Heywood said Tuesday night.
Washington voters have been asked 11 times over nearly a century to approve personal or corporate income taxes. The first vote, in 1932, was successful. But a 5-4 state Supreme Court decision in 1933 struck the measure down. Later measures failed, most recently in 2010 when the income thresholds were $200,000 for individuals and $400,000 for joint filers.
The income tax is a 9.9% tax on individual and household wage income above $1 million a year.  The state’s chief economist estimates the income tax will generate $3.5 billion from 25,000 filers in 2029, the first year of collections.
In addition to the ballot battle, there’s a pending lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of the tax. That case has effectively been on hold to see what voters do. Ferguson, a former three-term state attorney general, has consistently expressed confidence that courts would uphold the levy.
Just two years ago, Let’s Go Washington, the conservative political committee behind Initiative 645, qualified an initiative barring the state and local governments from taxing income. The Legislature adopted the measure only to set it aside earlier this year to allow for this income tax.
Washington’s tax system has long been considered among the most regressive in the country, meaning lower earners pay proportionally more of their income in taxes than wealthier households. This is largely due to the state’s heavy reliance on sales taxes and the lack of an income tax, according to policy experts. 
Until this year, Washington was one of only nine states nationwide that did not tax individual wage and salary income.

The disputed income tax was created by Senate Bill 6346, which the Legislature passed in March. It takes effect Jan. 1, 2028. The first dollars would start to arrive in 2029. 
Only a few paragraphs in the 110-page piece of legislation actually concern the income tax. Most of the text deals with how the money will be spent.
For example, the new law eliminates sales tax on diapers, personal hygiene products like soap and toothpaste, and some over-the-counter drugs. It also will repeal sales and use taxes for retail services, except advertising services, and expand a tax credit program for lower-income families. All this would happen in 2029 and the costs are to be covered from income tax collections.
Initiative 645 sought to repeal the income tax while preserving those elements.
Initiative foes forecast near ruination of the state’s social safety net and its ability to care for the most in need should those tax collections not materialize. They say the situation is already challenging with federal support for Medicaid and a host of social services getting cut.
They predicted the Legislature and governor would be forced to make deep cuts in all areas of state government to make ends meet.
Backers of the initiative countered that critics were trying to scare voters. They said because the first dollars would not arrive until 2029, the governor and lawmakers had time to find other ways to pay for the new commitments, or abandon them. 
The potential for the income threshold to drop below $1 million was an ongoing flashpoint.
Pro-initiative forces argued throughout the campaign that Democratic lawmakers would eventually levy the tax on households earning far less than $1 million because they will need the money. “Everybody knows it’s coming to that,”  Heywood said at a forum last month.
Late in the campaign, I-645 backers asserted retirees would see their pensions taxed because the law removed a prohibition on taxing pensions.
Ferguson has repeatedly vowed to veto any legislation that would lower the threshold.
The No on 645 campaign reported spending nearly $12.7 million as of Monday. Its biggest donors are the Service Employees International Union ($3.5 million), Washington Education Association ($3 million), Washington Federation of State Employees ($2.5 million), and National Education Association ($1 million).
Supporters had two primary committees pushing for passage of the initiative. 
One was Let’s Go Washington, which raised and spent more than $4 million. That sum included expenses to qualify the measure and separate initiatives concerning a ban on transgender girls’ participation in girls sports and parents rights.
The other committee was Vote Yes Repeal the Income Tax which reported $3.4 million in spending as of Monday. Lawrence Hughes, a retired businessman, is the largest donor at $750,000.

Other properties’ value could be assessed at no more than 4% more than the year […]
text:
Voters fill out ballots for the midterm election at the Millwood Field House on Tuesday in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma voters on Tuesday rejected a state question that would have limited increases in property taxes.
State Question 847 proposed a 1.75% cap on yearly growth in the taxable assessed value of a homestead or agricultural property. Other properties’ value could be assessed at no more than 4% more than the year before. This would have slowed how much property owners’ taxes increased over time.
Similar limits on property value growth, ranging from 0.35% to 1.75%, would have applied to Oklahomans over age 65 who earn too much income to qualify for a “senior freeze” that halts property tax increases.
The state Legislature put SQ 847 on the ballot to offer some amount of relief from rising costs, particularly for homeowners also struggling with skyrocketing home insurance premiums.
Critics have said the state question would deal a blow to funding for school districts and other public services without offering a way to replace the lost money.
The Oklahoma Tax Commission estimated local tax jurisdictions would have lost $45.78 million in expected property tax revenue over the first year had SQ 847 passed.
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, said concerns about the cost of property taxes were “very loud at the state Capitol” this year.
The state currently allows homesteads and agricultural land to increase by no more than 3% in assessed value per year and other properties to grow in valuation by no more than 5% annually. State lawmakers proposed the ballot measure to let voters choose whether they wanted to lower those caps.
“It looks like the voters of Oklahoma tonight said no,” Hilbert said at a GOP election watch party in Oklahoma City on Tuesday night. “They don’t want to see changes to property taxes, and so moving forward, we’ll take that into consideration.”

title: Property tax slash crosses approval threshold on election night
description: A far-reaching homestead property tax reduction proposed by the Legislature garnered the approval of more than 62% of the unofficial vote, besting the 60% approval required to be enshrined in the Florida Constitution.  At full implementation, state economists estimated Amendment 3 would reduce local revenues by as much as $12 billion annually. For well over [...]
text:
A banner advertising voting hangs outside the Leon County Courthouse on Aug. 12, 2024. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)A far-reaching homestead property tax reduction proposed by the Legislature garnered the approval of more than 62% of the unofficial vote, besting the 60% approval required to be enshrined in the Florida Constitution. 
At full implementation, state economists estimated Amendment 3 would reduce local revenues by as much as $12 billion annually.
For well over a year, Gov. Ron DeSantis has been advocating for eliminating property taxes, although he took about as long to propose a statutory language to do so. The Legislature amended his plan to protect property taxes collected for schools.
“Big win on Amendment 3 for Florida homeowners!” DeSantis posted Tuesday night, replying to a Republican Party of Florida post that categorized the amendment’s passage as “an incredible VICTORY for Florida homeowners!”
Amendment 3 had the support of the state GOP and Florida Realtors. In the days leading up to the election, DeSantis hosted events throughout the state advocating for the amendment. 
The Florida Democratic Party opposed the amendment, as did public safety and law enforcement groups, such as the Florida Sheriff’s Association, as well as outgoing Senate President Ben Albritton, a Republican from central Florida. 
Former state lawmaker Jeff Brandes campaigned against the amendment, and even led a lawsuit challenging its language.
“Florida passed Amendment 3. The governor and the Legislature own what comes next. They have the responsibility to manage the fallout,” he posted to social media Tuesday, going on to list cities and counties he says will struggle with passage of the amendment.
“Floridians voted for lower taxes, and they count on their communities for the basics,” Brandes wrote. “Both are reasonable expectations. The governor and the Legislature can honor that vote by giving cities and counties a clear plan before they write their next budgets, so every community can decide how best to keep the services its residents depend on.”
Amendment 1
Voters rejected an increase in the capacity of the state’s budget stabilization fund, the rainy-day account tapped in case of emergencies or revenue shortfalls. 
The proposal, Amendment 1, received just more than 40% support. 
That means the state will continue to maintain up to 10% of the previous year’s net revenue in the budget stabilization fund, instead of the 25% proposed by the amendment. 
DeSantis railed against the amendment, but the Republican Party of Florida endorsed it. 
“Amendment 1 — a testament to our failed former speaker of the House — is deservedly going down in flames. Good riddance,” DeSantis posted to X Tuesday evening. He referred to Speaker Daniel Perez, with whom he has feuded for two years.
Amendment 2
The other measure on the statewide ballot was Amendment 2, Exemption of Tangible Personal Property on Agricultural Land from Taxation. 
That amendment would have excluded farming equipment like tractors from assessed taxes, but as of Tuesday night had 58.25%. According to a state estimate, the amendment would’ve reduced local government revenue by about $31 million starting in 2027.
The Florida Farm Bureau supported the amendment.

name: California
title: Prop. 43: Should it be harder to raise local taxes for specific services?
description: California’s Prop. 43 would require two-thirds of votes to pass any local taxes that pay for specific services, such as wildfire prevention, education and healthcare.
text:
In summary
California’s Prop. 43 would require two-thirds of votes to pass any local taxes that pay for specific services, such as wildfire prevention, education and healthcare. 


Should California make it harder to pass local taxes designated for specific services?
That’s the question posed by Proposition 43, which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local special taxes, such as those paying for wildfire prevention, education and healthcare.
Californians already approved a two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes in 1996. So why do we need to vote on it again?
That’s because for decades, it was widely assumed that the requirement applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court ruled that it applied specifically to taxes that local officials put on the ballot. 
But the justices did not say whether the same requirement applied to citizen-driven tax measures, when individuals or groups gather enough signatures to put them on the ballot. Since then, several high-profile tax measures, such as the hefty Los Angeles tax on mansion sales and a Sonoma County sales tax to fund emergency response, passed with a simple majority.
Prop. 43 would not scrap existing taxes, but would apply to future tax initiatives. 
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, an anti-tax group that sponsored Prop. 43, argues the measure would close the loophole the court created and clarify that the requirement applies to all local special taxes. The two-thirds requirement has existed since 1849, when the state Constitution required a two-thirds vote for the state to borrow money, said Jon Coupal, president of the association. 
“The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.”
But local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates opposed the measure, arguing it would allow “minority rule” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes, making it harder for locals to connect revenue for essential services.
Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock to raising local funding, stressing that Los Angeles voters are voting this November on a half-cent sales tax to hire more firefighters. 
“The motivation behind Prop. 43 is clear. It’s the same motivation that is behind efforts to restrict mail voting and otherwise rig the system to prevent everyday citizens from having a say in their own government,” Roberts wrote in an op-ed.
Prop. 43 was sparked by opposition to the Los Angeles mansion tax, which added a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax, approved by 58% of voters in 2022, has generated $1.4 billion in revenue for the city. 
Anti-tax advocates and businesses fought the tax, arguing it impeded local development, including affordable housing. Earlier this year, Coupal championed an extensive ballot measure that would have retroactively canceled out the mansion tax, but reached a last-minute compromise with the Democratically-led Legislature to put Prop. 43 on the ballot instead. 
Democratic legislators voted for the deal but have urged voters to reject it. Assembly Appropriations Chair Buffy Wicks, an Oakland Democrat who wrote Prop. 43, said she wrote it merely to kill a worse proposal.
“The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” she said.
